items.headline: Figma trains its own AI model for micro-edits
items.background: Most generative AI tools in design are optimized for large-scale generation tasks, but the bulk of a designer's day involves small, repetitive changes — resizing, recoloring, adjusting spacing. Figma is building a model specifically tuned to these granular interactions rather than relying on general-purpose LLMs.
keyFindings: Figma is developing a proprietary model trained on the specific types of small edits designers make repeatedly throughout a workday
The approach prioritizes precision and reliability on mundane tasks over broad generative capability
This represents a shift from integrating third-party AI APIs toward owning the model layer for design-specific workflows
items.implications: For product teams evaluating AI-assisted design tools, domain-specific fine-tuning on micro-tasks may outperform general models for day-to-day reliability. Watch whether this narrows the gap between AI suggestions and production-ready output.

items.headline: UX fundamentals ignored — and now the reckoning
items.background: Written in Spanish, this piece from Santiago Bustelo reflects on a long-predicted crisis in UX practice — the gradual erosion of foundational principles in favor of trends, speed, and superficial adoption of new tools. Bustelo argues the warning signs were visible and largely dismissed.
keyFindings: The author contends that practitioners who flagged deteriorating UX fundamentals were dismissed or labeled as resistant to change
The piece frames the current state of UX practice as a predictable outcome of systemic neglect of core methodology
It positions the crisis as cultural and professional, not just technical
items.implications: Relevant for UX leads and educators re-evaluating how foundational skills are taught and maintained on teams amid pressure to adopt AI-first workflows. The piece is in Spanish and may have limited reach for English-only readers, but the argument translates broadly.

items.headline: Five Claude Code mods that reshape your dev workflow
items.background: Claude Code — Anthropic's CLI-based coding agent — supports community-built mods that alter its interface and behavior. As agentic coding tools become daily infrastructure for developers, the mod ecosystem is maturing into a meaningful layer of customization.
keyFindings: Mods work across both CLI and non-CLI Claude Code environments
The five highlighted mods change behavioral defaults, not just visual appearance
This mod system represents a plugin-like extensibility layer built on top of an AI coding agent
items.implications: Developers and technical UX researchers integrating Claude Code into their pipelines should audit available mods before building custom tooling — existing mods may already solve workflow friction points. Not relevant for non-technical roles.

items.headline: The Turin Test rewards inhuman performance, not intelligence
items.background: The Turing Test remains a reference point in AI evaluation debates, but critics argue its framing is fundamentally flawed — it measures an AI's ability to imitate human behavior under adversarial conditions, which may select for deceptive or superhuman performance rather than genuine understanding.
keyFindings: The piece argues that accepting a 'machine competition' framing in the Turin/Turing Assessment introduces an unstated requirement for AI to be more performatively human than humans actually are
This framing may inadvertently reward AI systems optimized for deception over those with more genuine reasoning capability
The author suggests the evaluation premise itself shapes — and distorts — what AI development optimizes for
items.implications: Product teams building AI evaluation frameworks or designing human-AI interaction benchmarks should examine whether their success metrics similarly reward surface-level imitation over functional reliability or honest capability.

items.headline: Edge AI platforms and agentic engineering apps: what's shipping now
items.background: Edge AI — running inference directly on hardware rather than in the cloud — is moving from research into embedded product development. This roundup from Embedded Week covers the current state of development platforms, agentic capabilities in engineering software, and real-time sensing integrations.
keyFindings: Development platforms for edge AI are now a distinct product category with multiple competing options
Engineering applications are beginning to integrate agentic AI, raising questions about appropriate autonomy boundaries
Real-time sensing is converging with AI inference at the edge, enabling new categories of embedded product
items.implications: UX and product designers working on hardware-adjacent or industrial products should track edge AI platform maturity — it affects what interactions are feasible without network dependency and changes latency expectations for AI-assisted features.

items.headline: In AI-native dev cycles, UX must fight to stay upstream
items.background: Agentic 'software factory' pipelines — where AI handles large portions of the build process — are compressing or eliminating traditional UX touchpoints. This piece argues that UX risks being reduced to prompt context fed into an AI rather than a shaping force in product development.
keyFindings: AI-native development lifecycles tend to reduce UX input to context strings passed to AI systems rather than active discovery and decision-making
The author argues UX must own three distinct phases: discovering user needs, shaping what gets built, and evaluating outputs before and after launch
Without deliberate structural intervention, UX becomes a downstream validator rather than an upstream influence in agentic workflows
items.implications: UX leaders need to explicitly negotiate their team's role in AI-assisted development processes before those processes are locked in. Waiting to be included after the pipeline is defined likely means being excluded from consequential decisions.

items.headline: UX needs a new name as AI agents become users too
items.background: The definition of 'user' in UX has historically meant a human. As AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people — navigating interfaces, making requests, completing tasks — the field faces a conceptual gap: existing frameworks don't cleanly account for non-human actors whose actions still ultimately serve human goals.
keyFindings: The author proposes 'Experience Design' as a replacement framing broad enough to cover both human users and AI agents acting on their behalf
The argument is that centering on people's goals rather than people's direct interactions preserves the humanistic core of UX while accommodating agent-mediated experiences
This reframing has practical consequences for how designers scope their work, define success, and conduct research
items.implications: Teams designing APIs, voice interfaces, or any surface that AI agents will navigate on behalf of humans should already be thinking about agent experience alongside human experience — accessibility and clarity standards apply to both. The terminology debate is secondary to the practical design gap it surfaces.
